name: E-commerce Directive
evidence_rating: thin: Commission evaluations are qualitative; no causal study isolates the Directive's or its safe harbours' effect on trade, investment or innovation; main quantitative estimate is industry-funded
summary: The E-commerce Directive set no measurable targets. The Commission's 2020 evaluation concluded that its core rules, including liability protection for online intermediaries, helped digital services grow across borders, but national courts applied them inconsistently; this led to the Digital Services Act. No independent study has measured the safe harbours' effect on investment or innovation in Europe; the best-known estimate is a Google-funded simulation.

indicators.objective: The 1998 proposal predates impact assessments and financial-statement indicators; no quantified targets were set. Art. 21 required a report every two years (only the 2003 report was issued); a full evaluation was annexed to the 2020 DSA impact assessment
Internal market for information society services
indicators.indicator: Free cross-border provision of online services under the country-of-origin principle
indicators.evidence: 2020 evaluation: the Directive 'enabled growth and accessibility of digital services cross-border' but there is clear evidence of legal fragmentation, national laws with extraterritorial effect and little use of the cooperation mechanism. No quantitative ex-post estimate of its effect on cross-border trade.

indicators.objective: Legal certainty for intermediaries (liability safe harbours)
indicators.indicator: Conditional liability exemptions for mere conduit, caching and hosting; no general monitoring obligation
indicators.evidence: 2020 evaluation: liability regime remains the 'key regulatory pillar' but conflicting national court interpretations create significant uncertainty; incentives favour removal over protecting legal content. No causal study of the EU safe harbours' effect on investment or innovation; the main quantitative estimate (Oxera 2015) is a Google-funded simulation.

indicators.indicator: Transparency and consumer-facing provisions build trust
indicators.evidence: 2020 evaluation: these provisions are still relevant and largely complied with, but not measured with outcome data.

literature.citation: European Commission (2003), First Report on the application of Directive 2000/31/EC on electronic commerce, COM(2003) 702
literature.title: First Report on the application of Directive 2000/31/EC on electronic commerce
literature.headline: Directive 'has had a substantial and positive effect on e-commerce within Europe' despite limited experience; revision premature
literature.summary_plain: Three years in, the Commission judged the Directive positive for online business but said it was too early to measure its effects.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Evaluation of the e-Commerce Directive (Annex 5 to the Digital Services Act impact assessment), SWD(2020) 348
literature.title: Evaluation of the e-Commerce Directive (Annex 5 to the Digital Services Act impact assessment)
literature.outcomes: cross-border services; legal certainty; fundamental rights
literature.headline: Core principles still valid; enabled cross-border growth of digital services; liability regime gave minimum legal certainty but conflicting national interpretations and fragmentation; only partially achieved protection of fundamental rights; cooperation mechanism little used
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own evaluation found the Directive's core rules helped online services grow across borders, but national courts applied them inconsistently and removal of legal content was not well protected.

literature.citation: Lomba & Evas (EPRS) (2020), Digital Services Act: European added value assessment, European Parliamentary Research Service, PE 654.180
literature.title: Digital Services Act: European added value assessment
literature.method: gap analysis plus macro-model simulation (Cambridge Econometrics E3ME)
literature.headline: Identified 22 gaps and risks in the e-Commerce Directive framework; reform packages on consumer protection/common e-commerce rules and on content management estimated to add about EUR 47bn and EUR 29bn to EU GDP over 2020-30
literature.summary_plain: The Parliament's research service estimated that fixing gaps in the e-Commerce Directive could add tens of billions of euros to EU GDP over a decade.

literature.citation: Oxera (2015), The economic impact of safe harbours on Internet intermediary start-ups, Oxera report prepared for Google
literature.title: The economic impact of safe harbours on Internet intermediary start-ups
literature.method: simulation model of start-up success (Chile, Germany, India, Thailand)
literature.headline: A clear, low-cost liability regime could raise intermediary start-up success rates by 4% (Chile) to 24% (Thailand); in Germany by 1.6 percentage points (about 9%), NPV +3%; results are order-of-magnitude only
literature.summary_plain: A Google-funded simulation estimated that clearer liability protection could make German internet start-ups about 9% more likely to succeed.
literature.quality: simulation with assumed parameters; not causal

literature.citation: Lefouili & Madio (2022), The economics of platform liability, European Journal of Law and Economics 53(3), 319-351
literature.title: The economics of platform liability
literature.venue: European Journal of Law and Economics 53(3), 319-351
literature.headline: Reviews platforms' incentives to curb misconduct without liability and how stricter liability would affect prices, terms, business models, investment, competition and third-party sellers; weighs costs and benefits of policy proposals
literature.summary_plain: An economics review finds that making platforms more liable for users' misconduct has both benefits and costs, including effects on prices, investment and competition.
literature.quality: review; partly based on a report for the European Commission

literature.citation: Erickson & Kretschmer (2020), Empirical Approaches to Intermediary Liability, in G. Frosio (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Online Intermediary Liability, OUP, 104-121
literature.title: Empirical Approaches to Intermediary Liability
literature.venue: in G. Frosio (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Online Intermediary Liability, OUP, 104-121
literature.method: systematic review of empirical studies on notice-and-takedown, 1998-2018
literature.headline: Rightholders make heavy use of notice-and-takedown, accelerated by automation since about 2012; abuse is real but probably overstated; due process and transparency need improvement
literature.summary_plain: A review of 20 years of research on safe-harbour takedown systems finds heavy and growing use, some abuse, and weak transparency.
